title: Flight 19 never comes home

facts.text: At about 2:10 p.m. on 5 December 1945, five TBM Avenger torpedo bombers took off from Naval Air Station Fort Lauderdale on a navigation training flight over the Bahamas. Fourteen Navy and Marine Corps airmen were aboard.

The instructor leading Flight 19 was Lt. Charles Carroll Taylor, USNR, 28, a combat veteran with about 2,500 flying hours. The ranking officer among the students was a Marine, Capt. Edward J. Powers Jr.

Around 4 p.m. another instructor in the air heard Taylor say both his compasses were out and he was trying to find Fort Lauderdale. Believing he was over the Florida Keys, Taylor led the flight northeast, further out to sea.
Weather worsened and night fell. At 7:04 p.m. Taylor's last words were heard: "when the first plane drops below ten gallons, we all go down together."
At 7:27 p.m. a PBM Mariner flying boat under Lt. (jg) Walter G. Jeffrey left Naval Air Station Banana River with 13 men to search for them. It sent one routine report and was never heard from again.

At 9:15 p.m. the tanker SS Gaines Mills reported a burst of flames, apparently an explosion, leaping about 100 feet and burning for ten minutes. The ship passed through a pool of oil and found no survivors. The carrier USS Solomons had watched a plane vanish from radar at the same place.
Air and sea searches from 6 to 10 December found no wreckage of any of the six aircraft and no trace of the 27 men.
The Navy board blamed Taylor. The chief of naval air training wrote that he had become so hopelessly confused as to have suffered "something akin to a mental aberration."
Taylor's mother, Katherine, refused to accept it. After her campaign, a Navy corrections board in 1947 changed the finding to say the flight disappeared "for reasons or causes unknown."

A 1964 Argosy magazine article, "The Deadly Bermuda Triangle," turned the loss into legend. NOAA says there is no evidence that disappearances happen more often there than in any other busy stretch of ocean.

photoNote: Tier: green. Five Grumman TBF Avengers of squadron VGS-29 in a stepped echelon over towering cumulus near Norfolk, Virginia, September 1942. U.S. Navy photo, National Archives 80-G-427475 (naId 520789), use Unrestricted, public domain. Saved 1577 x 1920 (portrait) from NARA's 2464 x 3000 TIFF. NOT Flight 19: it was taken three years earlier, of TBFs not the TBM-1C and TBM-3 aircraft Taylor's flight flew, and its wide use online (and as the Wikipedia infobox picture, captioned "a similar flight") has made many people think it shows the lost flight. The caption must say so. Chosen because five Avengers in formation is exactly what vanished, and the empty sky reads as foreboding. Runner up: the portrait of Lt. Charles C. Taylor (Commons File:Charles_C._Taylor.jpg, NAS Fort Lauderdale, marked U.S. Navy public domain, only 364 x 529, too small for a card).

declassified.fact: Flight 19 should have carried 15 men, not 14. One gunner, Corporal Allan Kosnar, asked to be excused from the exercise that afternoon, so Avenger FT-81 took off with its pilot and a single crewman.

body:
Lt. Charles Taylor radioed that both his compasses were out. Believing he was over the Florida Keys, he led five bombers further out to sea.

5 December 1945. Flight 19, five TBM Avengers with 14 airmen, had left Fort Lauderdale that afternoon on a training flight over the Bahamas. Night fell and the weather worsened. Taylor's last words were heard at 7:04 p.m.

A PBM Mariner flying boat sent to search, with 13 men aboard, also vanished. No wreckage of any of the six aircraft was ever found.

The Navy blamed Taylor. His mother, Katherine, fought the finding, and in 1947 it was changed to say the flight disappeared "for reasons or causes unknown." The photo shows Navy Avengers in 1942, not the lost flight.
